title: After Ganpati Visarjan, Where Does All the Waste Actually Go?
excerpt: Mumbai's first immersion round is done — 61,640 idols into artificial ponds and the sea. With the September 25 finale approaching, the city's waste machinery, and its controversies, swing into action.
body:
• After the one-and-a-half-day festivities, 61,640 idols were immersed in Mumbai by the morning of September 16, per BMC data — 61,247 household idols, 301 from public mandals and 92 Hartalika idols.
  • The final and largest immersion round falls on Anant Chaturdashi, Friday, September 25; Ganeshotsav 2026 began on September 14.
  • The BMC has built more than 275 artificial ponds and requires idols under six feet to use them, as Plaster of Paris idols and chemical paints remain the core pollution problem.
  • Idol makers and mandal organisers in Girgaon and Lalbaug are pushing back, asking for controlled sea immersion of small eco-friendly idols; the Bombay High Court has left the pond question to an expert monitoring committee.

Every September, Mumbai carries lakhs of Ganesh idols — worshipped for days in homes and pandals — to the water and lets them go. This year, the first immersion round is done: According to data released by the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation, 61,640 idols were safely immersed across the city by the morning of September 16, after the one-and-a-half-day Ganeshotsav festivities.

Households accounted for the overwhelming majority — 61,247 idols — alongside 301 from sarvajanik (public) mandals and 92 Hartalika idols of Goddess Parvati. Idols also go in on the fifth and seventh days, with the grand finale on Anant Chaturdashi, Friday, September 25, when the biggest mandals — Lalbaugcha Raja among them — process to the sea.

The Environmental Problem

Visarjan symbolizes Lord Ganesha's return to his heavenly abode, carrying away devotees' troubles. But the ritual has a material afterlife. Idols made of Plaster of Paris are not biodegradable and can take months to dissolve, while the chemical paints used to decorate them carry heavy metals like mercury, chromium and lead. Together they contaminate water bodies, damage aquatic life and degrade water quality — with health consequences for communities that depend on those waters.

Eco-friendly practice is growing — natural shadu mati (clay) idols, home immersion in buckets, natural paints — but PoP remains widespread, and the question of where the waste goes now defines the festival as much as the devotion does.

The Civic Machinery

The BMC's answer is scale. The civic body has constructed more than 275 artificial ponds across Mumbai, and court directions currently in force require all idols under six feet to be immersed in them rather than in natural water bodies. The corporation has also distributed 10,800 litres of eco-friendly paint and 3,000 litres of eco primer to sculptors on an experimental basis, and trained more than 1,000 volunteers from public Ganesh mandals in safety and emergency response. Devotees are urged to immerse small, nature-friendly idols at home, in buckets or society-level arrangements.

The Pushback

Murtikars (idol makers) and mandal organisers in Mumbai's Girgaon and Lalbaug — neighbourhoods where Ganeshotsav runs deepest — have asked the BMC to allow controlled sea immersion of small, eco-friendly idols, opposing the blanket rule for idols below six feet. Pradeep Maduskar, a 73-year-old murtikar from Girgaon, argued that most household and smaller mandal idols are already below six feet and made of shadu clay, and that regulating idol materials and colours would address pollution without banning sea immersion outright. Adhvait Pedhamkar of the Lalbaug Sarvajanik Utsav Mandal pointed to logistics: artificial ponds could face queues, traffic pressure and limited space on the main immersion days, when thousands of devotees descend at once.

The courts, for now, have stepped back. The Bombay High Court declined to fix the number of artificial ponds itself, entrusting that call to an expert monitoring committee. The BMC has made six truck-mounted immersion tanks available as a stopgap.

Where the Waste Goes

After each immersion round, the cleanup begins. Civic workers dredge and clear the artificial ponds of idol remains and debris so the ponds can be used again; at designated beaches, what the sea leaves behind is collected by BMC crews. The residue of PoP idols — which refuse to dissolve — is the hardest part of the job, which is precisely why the civic body keeps pushing idol makers toward shadu clay and natural paints. The festival's waste trail, in other words, ends where Mumbai's municipal system begins.

Diaspora Angle

Ganesh Chaturthi is celebrated by Indian communities from New Jersey to Singapore, and the eco-idol debate travels with it. Many diaspora mandals have already moved to clay idols and symbolic home visarjan in tubs — a quieter version of the same reckoning Mumbai is working through at scale.

What's Next

The real test comes on September 25, when Anant Chaturdashi brings the largest idols and the biggest crowds to the water. Watch the monitoring committee's calls on pond capacity, whether the six-foot rule holds through the final round, and how far the eco-paint experiment moves the needle on what the sea has to absorb.
